section_title: Why should Epaphroditus be welcomed with joy?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 25 But I thought it necessary to send back to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs. 26 For he has been longing for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill. 27 He was sick indeed, nearly unto death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow.

28 Therefore I am all the more eager to send him, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious. 29 Welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor men like him, 30 because he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life to make up for your deficit of service to me.

context_lines: Paul explains why he is sending Epaphroditus back. He describes him as a brother, fellow worker and fellow soldier, and as the Philippians’ messenger who ministered to his needs. [Philippians 4:18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/philippians/4.htm) identifies him as the person who brought their gifts.

Epaphroditus had been seriously ill, close to death. He was distressed because the Philippians had heard about his illness. Paul describes his recovery as God’s mercy toward both Epaphroditus and himself, sparing him further sorrow.

Sending him back is meant to bring joy to the community and ease Paul’s concern. Paul asks them to welcome him in the Lord and honor people like him because he risked his life in Christ’s work to provide the service they could not personally give.
The account makes the chapter’s concern for others tangible. Gifts, travel, illness, worry, recovery and a welcome home are all part of this shared service.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand Paul’s commendation as honoring costly, faithful service and the concern shared between this messenger and the church. [Wesley’s notes on verses 25–30](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-philippians/) explain the gifts, recovery and service offered on the community’s behalf. The [USCCB note on verse 25](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/philippians/2) likewise identifies him as their messenger sent to help Paul. His illness and recovery are described within the real affection and care of this relationship.
god_plan_lines: [1 Corinthians 12:24–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/12.htm) describes God arranging the body so its members care for one another: when one suffers, the others share the suffering, and when one is honored, they share the joy. That is a supported parallel to the concern and welcome described here.

The larger purpose includes a community that values and cares for the people who serve within it. Epaphroditus’s practical help matters to Paul’s gospel work, and his own needs matter to the community. God’s people are being formed into a body whose members belong to one another.
